source.title: Learned feature representations are biased by complexity, learning order, position, and more
source.authors: Andrew Kyle Lampinen; Stephanie C Y Chan; Katherine L. Hermann

record.file_problem: none noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports results on feature-representation strength and sparsity, but does not test superposition, feature overlap or direction geometry, capacity-based polysemanticity, LLM feature recovery, SAE canonicality, or feature dimensionality. It mentions superposition and SAEs in discussion, without testing them.
record.gate_note: The reported experiments measure how task-feature properties affect representation variance and representation sparsity. These measures do not establish whether sparse features overlap as near-orthogonal directions or test any other listed claim version. The paper mentions superposition and sparse dictionary learning as context and a limitation; those mentions are not experimental results.
record.test_reason: The paper measures how strongly features are represented (linear-regression R² of activations on feature values) and a coefficient-entropy sparsity score. These are measured in MLPs, small transformers and CNNs/ResNets trained on controlled multi-feature tasks. None of these measures shows whether more sparse features than dimensions are stored as overlapping near-orthogonal directions. Nor do they show capacity-driven polysemanticity, SAE recovery in LLMs, SAE canonicality, or feature dimensionality. Superposition appears only in the limitations, which note that linear analyses may miss superposed encodings. SAEs appear only in the discussion, as an untested argument that an ℓ2 reconstruction loss favours high-variance features. So the paper discusses the claim without testing it.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that learned representations are systematically biased by complexity, learning order, prevalence, output position and other properties, even when all features are learned well. They add that this complicates interpretability, PCA/visualization, RSA and model–brain comparisons. They do not draw conclusions about superposition.
record.recipe_differences: The paper measures feature variance explained and representation sparsity across controlled tasks; it does not apply the Toy Models of Superposition method or test overlapping feature directions.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcome varies with feature complexity, training order, feature prevalence, output position, architecture, optimizer, dropout, and task setup.

fits_no_version.finding: Feature representation strength (variance explained) is biased by feature complexity, learning order, prevalence, output position, number of output values, and architecture (e.g. ResNet shape bias vs CNN color bias). More complex features yield sparser decoding, even when all features are learned equally well.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In controlled multi-feature tasks, the share of representation variance a feature occupies depends on extraneous properties of the feature and the training process, not only on its computational role.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-unit analysis (App. B.4) shows penultimate MLP units carrying variance for both easy and hard features and for other inputs. Hard-feature signal concentrates in units that were initially easy-selective. This is a mixed-selectivity observation with no capacity pressure, but it is not measured as polysemanticity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual units can carry signal about multiple task features even when the network has far more units than features.

record.problems: The main experiments use controlled synthetic or constrained tasks and toy-scale models, not LLMs. The primary representation-strength analysis is based on linear regression; the paper notes that nonlinear or superposed encodings may not be captured by its linear analyses. The superposition discussion is not experimentally tested.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; the listed rows capture the directly relevant reported feature-representation strength and sparsity findings. Other downstream analyses and task-specific results were omitted because they do not bear on the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: No test of features exceeding dimensions, interference or overlap geometry, a sparsity-dependent phase transition, or regular geometry. The 'sparsity' measured is decoding-coefficient concentration, not input feature sparsity.
No manipulation of capacity relative to feature count, and no test of whether important features get dedicated dimensions while others share.

The per-unit analysis (App. B.4) shows units carrying variance from several features with only 2 task features in 64 units. The study does not frame or measure this as polysemanticity, and does not test causes of polysemanticity.
No LLMs are studied and no dictionary learning is run.
The argument that SAEs' ℓ2 loss biases them toward high-variance features is speculative; no SAE is trained or evaluated.
No comparison of 1-D and multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The SAE remark (§8) is a brief argument, not a result: SAEs trained with ℓ2 reconstruction may neglect low-variance features. It is relevant context for V5 completeness, but too speculative to count as T5. Rows are appropriately linked to none. Subject_kind 'toy_network' for ResNet-18 on synthetic images is acceptable given the small-scale synthetic setting.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test sparse features exceeding representational dimensions, overlap, near-orthogonality, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry.
Does not test polysemantic neurons or whether features compete for limited capacity and receive dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.
Does not measure feature distribution across neurons in LLMs or SAE recovery of sparse LLM features.
Discusses possible SAE reconstruction bias, but does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: 4-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Regressed penultimate-layer representations on easy linear and hard sum-of-4-inputs-mod-2 feature values; measured variance explained.

conditions.value: easy linear and hard sum of 4 inputs mod 2

rows.value: The easy feature dominates the penultimate representations; learning the hard feature increases the easy feature's variance explained.
rows.note: The text says both features reach perfect test accuracy; this measures relative representation strength, not superposition geometry.

rows.subject: 4-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Compared representation variance explained under simultaneous training and pretraining one feature to convergence before adding the other.

conditions.value: pretrain hard feature, then train easy feature
easy linear and hard sum of 4 inputs mod 2

rows.baseline: Simultaneous training; exact values not stated
rows.value: Pretraining the hard feature closes the gap somewhat, but the easy feature still dominates.
rows.note: This is a training-order effect on representation strength, not a test of feature sharing or overlap.

rows.subject: MLPs
rows.operation_detail: Compared representation variance for common and rare versions of easy and hard features.

conditions.value: common features present in 50% of data; rare features present in 10%
two linear and two sum-mod-2 features

rows.baseline: Common feature of equal difficulty; exact values not stated
rows.value: Less prevalent features explain less variance than more prevalent features of equal difficulty; the models achieve perfect accuracy across the features.
rows.note: Feature prevalence is measured; coactivation sparsity and direction geometry are not.

rows.subject: MLPs
rows.size_stated: 64 units in the analyzed penultimate layer
rows.operation_detail: Measured representation sparsity from the entropy of absolute logistic-regression decoding coefficients.
rows.baseline: Simpler features; exact values not stated
rows.value: More complex features tend to produce sparser representations, including when pretrained.
rows.note: This is sparsity of the learned representation by the paper's coefficient-based measure, not rarity of simultaneous feature activation.

rows.subject: Encoder-decoder transformers
rows.size_stated: 4 layers in each component; embedding size 128
rows.operation_detail: Measured feature variance explained at the final encoder representation and decoder pre-logit representation on character-sequence classification tasks.

conditions.value: exact-match, all-but-one, and sum-mod-2 sequence features

rows.baseline: Comparison among feature types; exact values not stated
rows.value: Encoder features explain relatively little variance; token extent and complexity affect the values. In the decoder, simpler features explain more variance, with some effect of token count.
rows.note: The study measures representation variance across sequence-task features, not superposition geometry.

rows.subject: Encoder-decoder transformers
rows.size_stated: 4 layers in each component; embedding size 128
rows.operation_detail: Measured representation variance by feature position in the output sequence.
rows.baseline: Later output positions; exact values not stated
rows.value: Features earlier in the output sequence are generally represented more strongly; position has little effect at the final encoder layer.
rows.note: Reports an output-position bias in a controlled sequence task.

rows.subject: Non-residual CNNs
rows.operation_detail: Measured variance explained by color, texture, and shape in representations of models trained on synthetic object images.

conditions.value: classify color, texture, and shape of single objects

rows.baseline: Texture and shape features; exact values not stated
rows.value: Color has a strong representation bias at the final spatial-pooling layer, weaker at the penultimate classifier layer.
rows.note: A vision-task representation-strength result; it does not measure feature overlap.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.size_stated: ResNet-18 followed by a two-layer MLP classifier
rows.operation_detail: Measured variance explained by color, texture, and shape in representations of models trained on synthetic object images.

conditions.value: classify color, texture, and shape of single objects

rows.baseline: Color and texture features; exact values not stated
rows.value: Shape is strongly favored in the representations, although color is easier and shape is the slowest feature to learn.
rows.note: The authors report an architecture-dependent reversal in representation bias.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
